units: the writer lost his source of income after a factory shut down
he turned to restoring old furniture
he writes his letter from the place where he practises his new trade
his savings are dwindling
that fall forces him to part with his pieces sooner than planned
he is learning to haggle over prices without embarrassment
each mended object brings him new buyers
he states that dread has left him since the change
he asks the woman he writes to for a reply
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the workshop where my tools now live. When the factory shut its doors my wage went with them, and that loss opened a door I would never have pushed at unaided. I could not bear the waiting, so I retrained and turned to the restoration of old furniture. Wood asks for patience, and it has handed mine back to me. My savings are thinning, which forces me to sell each piece earlier than I intended, and so I am learning to haggle without blushing. Every item I mend brings two more buyers to the door, and that small chain keeps me upright. You will ask whether I miss the old wage. I shall tell you the dread has gone, and that this quiet outweighs the security I surrendered. Write back to me soon. I need your voice the way glue needs a steady hand to press it.

units: a firm can run short of cash even with a full order book
the gap between money coming in and payments to suppliers creates the trouble
negotiating a deposit at the time of order eases the accounts at once
short-term credit suits only a passing shortfall
borrowing applied to a lasting imbalance merely hides the harm
putting occasional tasks out to contract lightens fixed costs
the margin must be examined product by product
a range sold at a loss can swallow the profit made on the others
the gap between money in and money out must be checked every week
text: What happens when a firm settles its suppliers long before its own sales are paid for? That gap drains the cash and chokes the business, however full the order book may look. Which measure works fastest? Reworking the terms: a deposit taken when the order is placed eases the bank account at once. Should the firm borrow instead? Short-term credit suits a passing shortfall, not a settled imbalance; applied to a structural fault, it merely hides the fever. How can fixed costs be lightened? By putting occasional jobs out to contract rather than keeping a workshop half idle. And if the trouble persists? Then the margin must be examined product by product, since one range sold at a loss swallows the profit made on the rest. Which figure deserves watching? The gap between money in and money out, checked every week, long before the yearly accounts.

units: a head of human resources sets out two options to the staff representative
the first option is to take on seasonal hands
the second option is to leave the extra load with the existing teams for higher pay
the representative holds that recruitment costs more in training

the head accepts that letting people go quickly would harm the firm's name
the representative counters that exhaustion cannot be ended like a contract
both sides settle on a middle course of limited extra hands and a bonus
a further meeting is planned before the season ends
text: The head of human resources set out his thinking to the staff representative, and put two courses before him. The first was to take on seasonal hands to absorb the rise in orders. The second was to leave the extra load with the teams already in post, paid at a higher rate. The representative answered that the first course cost more in training, while the second wore down the people who were there. The head accepted that letting workers go at the first slack spell would leave the firm with an ugly name, whereas an overload can be put right within a week. The representative countered that exhaustion, unlike a contract, cannot simply be ended. Both men settled on a middle course: a limited intake of extra hands, together with a bonus for the longer hours. They will meet again before the season closes.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the porter moved bales between the harbour and the warehouse
his pay depended on the weight he carried
the broker brought sellers and buyers together without touching the goods
the sworn weigher guaranteed the accuracy of the scales
the money changer exchanged coin come from elsewhere and took a share
the crier announced fresh arrivals in public
the scribe kept the register of debts
these trades have vanished or taken another name
each of these functions answered a lasting need of trade
text: Before machines took over, trade rested on callings whose names have faded from use. The porter hauled bales between the quayside and the warehouse; paid by the weight he carried, he wore out his back before middle age. The broker never laid a hand on the goods: he brought together a seller keen to clear his stock and a wary buyer. The sworn weigher stood behind the accuracy of the scales, and without him no bargain would have held. The money changer turned coin from elsewhere into coin that would pass here, and kept a share as he did so. The crier called out fresh arrivals in the square, there being no other way to advertise. The scribe, at the end of it, wrote down what was owed, since one man's memory rarely suited another's. Such work has gone or taken other names, yet each answered a need that trade has never stopped feeling.

units: at the start the owner lives off his savings and waits for buyers
the first visitors look without buying anything
a hard stretch follows in which money goes out faster than it comes in
half of the shops close during that stretch

these regulars come back every week
word passed between neighbours then brings in new buyers
the owner ends up taking on a hand
the text insists on the slowness of the process and the absence of any miracle recipe
text: Wondering what becomes of a corner shop in the weeks after it opens? At first the owner lives off his savings: he pays the rent, fills the shelves and waits. In the early weeks the custom is mostly the merely curious, who wander in, have a look round and leave without buying. Then comes a harder stretch, when money goes out faster than it comes in, and that is where half of these shops pull the shutters down for good. If the owner holds on, a core of loyal buyers gradually builds up, households that come back week after week. From then on, a word passed over the garden fence carries the business along without him. In the end, once the slope eases, he takes on an assistant and gets his breath back. Nothing miraculous about any of it: a long hill, and two good legs to climb it with.

units: a fire destroyed a textile warehouse without injuring anyone
the rolls of cloth meant for three neighbouring workshops were lost
the workshops stopped their machines for want of material
the seamstresses paid by the piece went unpaid
a distributor cancelled its seasonal order
that cancellation removed the workshops' main source of income
a manager describes a week of unbroken telephone calls
the insurer covers the goods but not the lost contracts
owners in the trade now split their stock between two distant warehouses
text: A fire in a textile warehouse brought a whole supply chain to a halt, and the shock ran further than anyone thought it could. Nobody was hurt, but the rolls of cloth held there for three neighbouring workshops were lost. With no fabric coming in, those workshops shut down their machines; with nothing made, they had no way of paying the seamstresses, who earn by the piece. Further along, a distributor cancelled its seasonal order, stripping the same workshops of their main source of income. The manager of one site says the telephone rang without a break for a week, every call bringing one more consequence. The insurer will cover the cloth, but not the contracts that melted away. Since then, owners across the trade have split their stock between two warehouses far apart, a cost they had dismissed as needless.

units: the difficulty comes from the awkwardness of naming a sum out loud
the advice is to gather one's results on a single sheet
those results must be measured in output or in customers won
the request must be made during a quiet spell
the eve of a deadline must be avoided
the request is put in one short sentence followed by a silence
the silence must be left to the other person
if the answer is no one must ask what conditions would make agreement possible
the asker comes back on the agreed day with his notes
text: Asking for a rise is like crossing a narrow footbridge: the run-up counts as much as the footing. Everyone knows the difficulty, and it lies in the awkwardness that grips the voice at the moment a sum must be named. Here is how to go about it. Gather first, on a single sheet, what you have achieved since you took the post, measured in output or in customers won. Choose next a quiet spell, never the eve of a deadline. Put your request in one clean sentence, then hold your tongue: the silence that follows belongs to the person across the desk, and you must not fill it. If the answer is no, do not argue; ask what conditions would make agreement possible, and write them down with care. Come back on the agreed day, sheet in hand. Patience is not shyness: it keeps the rope taut without snapping it.

units: two neighbouring employment areas responded differently to the same industrial decline
the first drew in vast storage and distribution sheds
that first area shows a recovered level of activity but low wages
its workforce turns over quickly
the second area funded workshops repairing machinery
recovery there was slower but median earnings are higher
both areas received equivalent public support
the length of training explains the gap between the two models
elected representatives are now studying the method they used to criticise
text: Two neighbouring employment areas have met the same industrial decline with opposite results, to the plain surprise of those who study them. The first went after vast storage and distribution sheds; its level of activity is back, but wages are flattened and the workforce turns over fast. The second chose to fund small workshops repairing machinery; its recovery came slower, and yet median earnings there now sit above those of its neighbour. Both received much the same public support, which rules out any explanation drawn from budgets. The gap rests first on the skill demanded: a sorting job is learned in a week, a repairer's craft takes two seasons. So the second area keeps its workers, while the first watches them move on. The elected representatives are now studying the method whose slowness they used to mock.

units: the hall stands on a slab worn down by passing feet

those stalls are held by families settled there for generations

a coffee counter takes the opposite side and serves as a place to exchange news about prices

the sloping floor carries the washing water out to a gutter outside
text: The covered market hall stands on a slab worn smooth by barrows and by boot leather. Along the north side stand the vegetable growers, their crates stacked behind them like a low wall. Down one of the side walls run the cheese and preserve stalls, held by families who have passed them on for generations. Opposite, under a patched glass roof, gather the sellers of cloth, thread and buttons. The far side holds a coffee counter, where traders settle their accounts and swap news about prices. A central aisle, wide enough for two carts, divides these quarters and carries the buyers through. At the back, a glazed office houses the keeper of the hall, who allots the pitches and collects the fee owed. The floor, gently sloped, sends the washing water out to a gutter beyond the doors.

units: at first the working week had no legal limit

after the limit came output rose
the writer explains that rise by the cost of tiredness
the weekly day of rest was fought with the same arguments
paid time off met the same opposition
none of the collapses announced at each step took place
the same arguments now serve against a shorter week
the writer accepts that an old line of reasoning may cease to hold
he demands that those who repeat a contradicted forecast explain why it failed
text: Shorter hours are forever set against the survival of firms, and the quarrel gains from being put back in order of time. At the outset the working week ran on with no legal bound, and employers swore that any limit would ruin the workshop. The limit came; output rose, because tiredness cost more than absence. Then came the weekly day of rest, condemned in the same terms, and after it paid time off, fought with equal heat. Each step carried its own forecast of widespread collapse, and each forecast was proved wrong. We now hear those very sentences again, aimed at a shorter week. A word of caution: nothing guarantees that an argument sound yesterday is sound still. But whoever repeats a prophecy already contradicted three times over owes us, at the very least, some account of why it failed.
